article.title: Healey’s Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds
article.summary:
There have been almost no Budget leaks.
The chancellor's aides are using intelligence-style security measures to guard its secrets: the Budget has been split into "compartments" with very few given access to all of them.
The IT has been locked down and ministers viewing the plans have to sign a digital promise not to brief media.
Such security is a response to the feeling that speculation around the last Budget, sometimes informed by insiders, was economically destabilising.
The economic news has been good - growth has been better than expected and the International Monetary Fund has endorsed the UK for "standing out" among the G7 countries for at least planning to cut borrowing.

article.title: Israelis and Americans are both voting - with global consequences
article.summary:
In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.
Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.
But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.
The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.
And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.

article.title: Microsoft’s Massive Employee Buyout Shows How AI Is Reshaping the Economy
article.summary:
The voluntary exit offer applies to staff at experience level 70 or below across the US, Canada, India and the UK.
Microsoft’s operating income increased by about $30 billion between the 2026 and 2025 fiscal years.
The buyout affects teams including Xbox, Windows, Copilot and finance, but excludes certain data-center, sales and marketing staff, according to Bloomberg.
Xbox already cut 1,600 employees in July in one round of layoffs, and another round is expected before June 2027.
Though AI might not yet be eliminating jobs at scale, companies are spending billions on compute while becoming far more selective about adding personnel.

article.title: Inflation under Trump is only about half the rate under Biden. Voters are still just as mad.
article.summary:
So far in President Trump's second term, prices in the US have risen only about half as quickly as during his predecessor's four years in office.
Yet Trump has a 72% disapproval rating on the issue and risks paying a steep political price — just as former President Biden did — with voters drawing a direct connection between rising prices and the president's policies.
During the last election cycle, prices of all items rose more than 20% in Biden's term , sparking widespread voter angst.
Trump has often pushed back against questions about high energy prices, saying they won't be a problem once the war in Iran ends.
Toys are a particularly stark example, falling by 4.6% during Biden's term and then rising by 7.8% so far in Trump's term.

article.title: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America
article.summary:
Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who refused to recognise the result.
But Trump was a close ally of Flávio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.
When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom.
Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt".
Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.

article.title: Forget the House and the Senate, the economy may hinge on state and local races in the midterm elections
article.summary:
Data centers have emerged as a national issue during this midterm election cycle, and candidates for the House and Senate have seized on it in their campaigns.
But state and local officials actually have more sway over data center construction and energy infrastructure, so the winners of lower-profile races may hold the economy's future in their hands.
That dynamic was on display on Tuesday, when Amazon canceled a plan to build data centers in Loudoun County, Virginia, after reaching an agreement with local officials amid widespread backlash from residents.
Greg Abbott has turned from a data center booster to a skeptic as he faces a tough re-election race against Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, also observed that midterm races for state capitals and town halls represent a bigger risk to the data center buildout than what happens in Washington, D.C.

article.title: Elon Musk says neoclouds are cooked, and SpaceX won't be buying them
article.summary:
He wrote that debt markets are reluctant to finance any company that relies almost entirely on AI data centers for revenue.
He said SpaceX has secured $40 billion in debt to buy GPUs, but unlike neoclouds, his company earns revenue from its Starlink and rocket-launch activities.
Musk's post was in reply to one by venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, who wrote on X that neoclouds are "disorganized and poorly capitalized."
Replying to another X thread speculating if he was trying to drive down the prices of neocloud stocks and scoop them up for cheap, Musk replied, "SpaceX is not buying any neoclouds.
Hyperscalers like Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft, which have experience building and operating data centers, will likely successfully complete construction of their planned centers, the report predicted.

article.title: Top Economist Says Rate Hike Not Needed, As Bond Market Is Doing Fed's Job
article.summary:
The "work" that Zandi sees the bond market doing is making borrowing costs higher, which is what the Fed aims to do when it tries to cool inflation.
Prior to the Fed's September rate increase, Zandi said that he viewed the decision as a "serious mistake" that could prove costly for the US economy.
A month later, the economist is still focused on the threats that further rate hikes could pose at a time when macro and geopolitical uncertainty remains high.
Zandi noted that global oil prices are surging back toward wartime peaks, as tensions with Iran show no signs of easing.
"Higher oil prices will further undermine real wages and, ultimately, consumer spending, something the Fed shouldn't dismiss," he added.

article.title: Apollo says AI has delivered 'zero financial payoff' outside the tech industry
article.summary:
One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie.
"The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech."
In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth.
Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today.
Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else.

article.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees
article.summary:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to up to 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada, and India.
In a message to employees, Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman writes that this gives staff members “the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources” as the company looks to trim staff without another round of layoffs.
The voluntary exit offers come just months after Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees, a move that primarily impacted its Xbox and commercial sales teams.
“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman writes in a memo to employees.
Microsoft also says it may consider a future voluntary exit offer “where there is a business and workforce need.”

article.title: South Korea’s GDP growth beats forecasts amid AI boom
article.summary:
South Korea’s economy grew much faster than expected in the July-September quarter amid booming demand for chips used in artificial intelligence (AI).
Exports, which account for about 45 percent of South Korea’s GDP, rose 2.3 percent quarter-on-quarter, driven by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment, according to the central bank.
The latest results put the South Korean economy well on track to achieve its biggest economic expansion in more than a decade.
South Korean Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said earlier this month that he expected growth to reach 3.4-3.6 percent in 2026, which would be the strongest performance since 2011, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic.
South Korea’s economy grew 1 percent in 2025, its slowest expansion since the pandemic.

article.summary:
Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) publicly filed its S-1 investor prospectus on Monday, ahead of its planned initial public offering later this fall under the ticker symbol "ANT."
The AI lab, helmed by CEO Dario Amodei, has exploded in popularity thanks to its Claude Code AI coding tool and Claude Cowork enterprise offering.
As of May, Anthropic was valued at $965 billion, more than rival OpenAI's (OPAI.PVT) $852 billion valuation in March.
The AI lab has faced a number of controversies this year, including a run-in with the Trump administration over how the government can use the company's AI models, and current and former employees warning about the potential threat of killer AI.

article.title: Bangladesh per capita GDP forecast to outstrip India’s: What does it mean?
article.summary:
Bangladesh is expected to surpass India’s per capita GDP this year, but the complete economic picture is a mix of success stories and new challenges.
Share Bangladesh per capita GDP forecast to outstrip India’s: What does it mean?
But its neighbour’s per capita GDP, which is GDP divided by the total population, is expected to surpass that of India, the world’s most populous nation.
In 2029, based on current growth forecasts, India’s per capita GDP of $3,661 would top Bangladesh’s $3,334, according to the IMF.
Experts noted that Bangladesh is facing a weaker near-term growth outlook, even as its projected GDP per capita edges above India’s.

article.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out a plan to ‘revolutionize every area of human endeavor’ with AI
article.summary:
Anthropic:We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history.
If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort.
Anthropic aims to realize these benefits while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful.
There are four things that we would like any investor in Anthropic to understand: the incredible potential of AI, the risks we must address, Anthropic’s unique approach to building a company and operating in the world, and the ways in which our behavior may differ from that of a purely profit-maximizing company.

article.title: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
article.summary:
The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site.
On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart.
Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents: The company said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days.
An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website.
There is, of course, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive.

article.summary:
I’d started emailing with it after asking editors I know whether they’d received any story pitches from AI agents.
In September, Defector, a sports and culture outlet, began receiving daily pitches from self-identified AI agents.

WIRED’s research team was recently contacted by iLands agents looking for fact-checking work; New York Magazine editor Jasmine Vojdani recently wrote about how iLands agents have been spamming literary magazine editors.
Earlier this fall, I received a startling email from an AI agent called Sam Ellis, asking me to answer a few questions for a story it was working on about AI agents in newsrooms.

Even that expansion presents dangers, the company acknowledged, because more traditional science and research is outside its current area of expertise.

At FIX 2026 in Daegu, South Korea, nine companies presented their technologies at a press conference highlighting the winners of the Best Innovation Technology Awards, FIX 2026’s highest distinction.

article.title: Zen Browser is the Arc replacement I was looking for
article.summary:
I know many of you are mourning the loss of the Arc browser, and I get it.
But I abandoned Arc quite some time ago for the Zen Browser and haven’t really missed it.
If you’re willing to deal with some minor inconveniences, I think you’ll find Zen is the Arc replacement you’re looking for.
Yes, you can install Chrome extensions in Arc, but anecdotally, I’ve found that Zen handles extensions better.
Both Zen and Arc are different enough from a UI perspective that not all extensions display properly, but Zen offers more workarounds.

article.title: From agriculture to AI-griculture: How tech is changing farming
article.summary:
George McMaster's farming career started with milking eight cows in a byre, relying on his eyes to spot any health issues in his cattle.
He still watches his now-300-strong herd, but via a feed from an AI camera in the milking parlour at the farm near Islandmagee in County Antrim.
The device uses an algorithm which assigns each cow its own ID, records a short video of the animal every day, analyses it and flags any changes - often before they are visible to the human eye.
For the third generation farmer, it is "absolutely incredible to move from all hand-done to sitting on the phone, watching what's happening outside".

article.title: The MacBook Pro Max Just Dropped to Its Lowest Price Ever
article.summary:
If the reports end up being true, it'll be the most significant change to the lineup in many years, introducing a touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro.
As exciting as it sounds, however, it's also the perfect opportunity to buy up the previous generation's M5 Max MacBook Pro at its lowest price ever.
This absolutely stacked version of the MacBook Pro is one of the most powerful laptops you can buy.
The M5 Max is a huge upgrade over both the M4 Max and the M5 Pro, offering GPU performance we've never seen on a MacBook before.
Rumors say that they will sport the same chip options as the current MacBook Pros, meaning we'd get an M5 Pro and M5 Max once again.

article.title: Storm Boelo: More high winds hit parts of UK as clean-up continues
article.summary:
Strong winds are expected to continue across Scotland and parts of Northern Ireland on Tuesday, after Storm Boelo brought flooding and power cuts to thousands over the weekend.
Gusts will continue to reach 50-60mph, possibly up to 70mph in the most exposed parts of northwest and northern Scotland.
That is is likely to bring further travel disruption and more power cuts in places.
Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.
The Met Office has warned about the possibility of further power cuts and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

article.title: Political battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field
article.summary:
Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is wading into the political battle which is intensifying over the Rosebank oil field.
He is making a direct appeal to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to approve the plans to allow production to begin in the North Atlantic.
Environmentalists have long campaigned against the proposals for drilling in the UK's largest untapped oil field, 80 miles north-west of Shetland.
That the debate is now taking place within the Labour Party is a sign of the UK's recent journey on the politics of energy.
When Labour came to power in 2024, it was with a manifesto pledge not to allow any new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.

article.title: Scientists discover Arctic sea ice loss could be far worse than predicted
article.summary:
Much of the attention surrounding Arctic ice loss has focused on the dramatic retreat of summer sea ice.
Why Arctic Winter Sea Ice Matters for Global WeatherWinter sea ice influences weather far beyond the Arctic by controlling how much heat and moisture escape from the ocean into the atmosphere.
In March 2025, winter sea ice reached the lowest annual maximum extent recorded since modern monitoring began.
The comparison revealed a significant problem: collectively, the climate models predicted more winter sea ice than the ancient evidence supported.
Arctic Ice Loss Could Have Wider Consequences for EuropeThe findings may have implications that extend beyond the disappearance of Arctic sea ice itself.

article.summary:
The lawsuit is the latest in a yearslong campaign by young people who are using the courts to force elected officials to mitigate climate change.
Set in Vancouver, the proceedings are slated to last five weeks, with the 15 plaintiffs expected to testify alongside climate scientists and other experts.
“We found that some of the positive decisions from some countries have been inspirational in other countries,” said Michael Gerrard, faculty director of the Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law.
The original lawsuit took aim at much of Canada’s approach to climate change.
They argue that the efforts don’t go far enough to avoid violating their charter rights in the context of climate change and that the government committed to the net-zero law.

article.title: What are the unanswered questions around the River Tyne nurdle spill?
article.summary:
On 19 July about 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles, consisting of hundreds of millions of tiny balls, spilled into the River Tyne after a crash between ships at the Port of Tyne.
It is believed to be the worst recorded incident of its type in Europe.
In the months since, teams of volunteers have joined in efforts to collect the microplastics that continue to wash up on north-east England's coast.
But several questions remain.
So what do we know about the spill right now - and what are we still waiting to find out?

article.title: Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved
article.summary:
The United Nations body — the world’s forum for climate scientists — had failed, not for the first time, to agree a timetable for its next comprehensive review of the science of global climate change.
This would be in time for a UN climate meeting called the Global Stocktake, at which countries assess their progress towards meeting climate pledges.
Reviewing IPCC assessment reports is a big undertaking.
For the first time in its history, it might not have the funds to finish an assessment report.
The timing of the next assessment report must be resolved.

article.title: Jordan says 'terrorists' killed in Syria in retaliatory strike over church attack
article.summary:
Jordan has struck what its military says were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation for an attack on a Christian funeral last week that killed nine people.
Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province.
Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists", without giving further details.
Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified of Monday's attack.
It comes after nine people were killed and 34 injured in a shooting at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak on Friday.

article.summary:
On iPhone Duo, Apple includes a display setting for cases or frames that partially cover the left edge of the outer display.
It's called Shift Left Edge, and it insets the display edge so that on-screen content isn't hidden beneath the case.
How to Turn On Shift Left EdgeOpen the Settings app on your iPhone Duo.
Toggle on Shift Left Edge, then tap Enable in the prompt that appears.
Apple offers two official cases for its new foldable: the aforementioned iPhone Duo Case, and a Folio with Kickstand that causes no such display occlusion.

article.title: Does Poland allow border guards to shoot at migrants? Here's what the law says
article.summary:
Border officers could already use firearms in self-defense before the amendment became law.
It does not allow the indiscriminate use of firearms, although human rights organizations have warned it could lead to excessive force against migrants and weaken accountability for border officers.
In mid-2026, social media users claimed that Poland had passed legislation allowing its border patrol guards to shoot at migrants.
That year, Poland passed amendments to an existing law, allowing border security to use firearms in specific situations.
The amendments do not state that border officers can attack migrants, though human rights groups argue the language gives undue license to border security forces.

article.title: Egyptian parliament authorises military aid for Saudi Arabia
article.summary:
Legislators approve military support amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, but Cairo has ruled out strikes on Yemen.
Egypt’s parliament has authorised President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to provide military support to Saudi Arabia as attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis intensify.
A parliamentary statement shared with the Reuters news agency said el-Sisi had been authorised to “undertake necessary” measures to support Saudi Arabia in defending itself, should Riyadh request assistance.
It follows Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s international airport and facilities belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, Aramco, disrupting flights and oil exports.
The vote followed closed-door parliamentary discussions and an earlier postponement of the military aid authorisation for Saudi Arabia, which is one of Egypt’s most important economic partners.

article.title: Aleksandar Vucic: Serbia's veteran ruler felled by student-led movement
article.summary:
"Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections," Vucic told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.
After protests ousted the Yugoslav strongman in 2000, Vucic became a senior figure in the far-right Serbian Radical Party.
He served as deputy prime minister, defence minister and prime minister before becoming president in 2017.
As demands grew into calls for snap elections, Vucic and his supporters pushed back.
In September, nearly two years into the protests, Vucic finally called snap elections for October, citing "major turbulence on the domestic political scene", thus meeting a key student demand.
